newsitem.title: USA: Cold weather pushes energy and grain prices higher.
newsitem.headline: Cold weather pushes energy and grain prices higher.

text.p: Snowstorms and bone-chilling cold temperatures that clamped down on the central United States at the weekend sent energy prices soaring on Monday.

Natural gas and heating oil prices led the surge on speculative buying and the cold also prompted some buying in wheat on worries about damage to the winter crop recently planted from Texas through the High Plains.
Overall, the buying interest helped push the Knight Ridder Commodity Research Bureau Index of 17 futures contracts up 1.80 points to close at 245.58.

Low U.S. natural gas inventories and expectations that more arctic air will sweep into the United States from Canada this week helped drive New York Mercantile Exchange January natural gas futures up 16 percent to a record high.
The January contract, which rallied to the record high of $4.56 per million British thermal units late in the day, finished 61.6 cents higher at $4.467.
January heating oil at NYMEX rose a strong 3.11 cents a gallon to 74.82 a gallon and January gasoline rose 2.48 cents at 69.52 cents a gallon.
January crude oil ended $1.27 at $25.74 a barrel higher after setting a new life-of-contract high at $25.95 during the day. A post-Gulf War high of $26.10 was made on Oct. 22.
"The whole oil complex is up on the weather," said Warren Tashnek, vice president at Fimat USA Futures in Houston.
Forecasters say cold will ice the United States from the Rocky Mountains to the Appalachians this week, with sub-zero Fahrenheit temperatures extending deep into Texas.
The bone-chilling cold should last into next week and drive up home heating costs.
"Natural gas usage in the Midwest will skyrocket," said Joel Burgio, a meteorologist with Weather Services Corp.
Snow from the system should largely remain in northern Iowa, Minnesota and the Dakotas, with accumulations of one to four inches a day through Wednesday, Burgio said.

The American Petroleum Institute said on Dec. 6 that U.S. heating oil stocks were 12.6 million barrels below the levels of a year ago. So prospects of high heating oil demand eclipsed news of the first Iraqi crude shipments in six years.
The first oil to flow from a United Nations oil-for-food deal was on a tanker carrying 153,500 metric tons of crude which left the Turkish Mediterranean port of Ceyhan on Monday.
Iraqi Oil Minister Muhammad Rasheed said on Sunday that Iraq had signed oil contracts with 11 foreign firms including some in the United States.

Cold U.S. temperatures extended into Texas and the Florida citrus belt also saw cooler weather. But orange juice markets showed no panic, with March orange juice at the New York Cotton Exchange ending down 1.05 cents a pound at 94.95 cents.
"It looks like the cold front is supposed to be affecting areas outside the citrus belt," said PaineWebber Inc. analyst Bernard Savaiko.
The cold and good export demand pushed wheat prices up at the Chicago Board of Trade, leading grain markets higher. December wheat rose 7-3/4 cents a bushel to end at $4.13-3/4.

Agronomists said the cold air probably will not cause much damage to the U.S. wheat crop, despite the lack of insulating snow cover in many regions. But U.S. wheat inspected for export in the week ended Dec. 12 totalled 17.157 million bushels, above trade estimates for 12-16 million bushels.
"Good export numbers, they were all above expectations," said Ron Kucha of O'Connor & Co.
